Period schedule:

Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

section_titles: Line of symmetry and mirror line
periods.activity_title: Ink-blot fold: discovering mirror halves in colour

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 1. Ink Design, p.164
tasks_in_class.description: Fold a sheet of paper in half, sprinkle water-colour drops at the fold, press to spread colour, open and observe the symmetrical ink design produced.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Making a paper airplane (a)–(c), p.165
tasks_in_class.description: Mark the line of symmetry in Fig. 3, 4, and 5; count how many lines of symmetry Fig. 8 has; decide where to place a mirror to see the right-half reflection and whether it matches the left half.

time_bands.activity: Distribute a sheet of paper and water colours to each student. Students fold the sheet in half and sprinkle or drip two or three small drops of colour near the fold line, then press the two halves firmly together and rub. Students open the sheet and look at the design: Let Us Do, 1. Ink Design, p.164 ("Fold paper, sprinkle colour drops, press, open and observe...."). Ask students to describe what they see — same on both sides, different, mixed — and introduce the phrase 'line of symmetry' for the fold.

Students fold a fresh sheet step by step to make a paper airplane following the textbook diagrams. At each of three folding stages they pause to mark the line of symmetry on that stage and count symmetry lines on the finished plane: Let Us Do, 2. Making a paper airplane (a)–(c), p.165 ("Mark line of symmetry in Fig. 3, 4, 5; count symmetry lines...."). Pairs then hold a small mirror along the fold line of their completed plane and confirm whether the reflected half matches the other side.

Whole-class gallery moment: four or five students hold up their ink-blot designs and the class identifies the line of symmetry by eye. The teacher draws two or three sample designs on the board and asks: 'If I fold here, do the halves match exactly?' Students vote and explain their reasoning, consolidating the vocabulary 'line of symmetry' and 'mirror line' as two names for the same thing.

Quick oral round: the teacher holds up each student's ink-blot and asks one child to point to the mirror line. Students check by re-folding. Close with the question 'What does a mirror line do to a shape?' — students respond in their own words, anchoring the concept before moving on.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have worked with rangolis and masks in Grade 3 already carry an intuitive sense of matching halves — build explicitly on that by naming the ink-blot fold as the same action. A common error at this stage is marking the mirror line anywhere a design looks 'pretty' rather than where the two halves are exact reflections; pause to check with re-folding whenever a student seems unsure. Keep water-colour quantities small to avoid long drying waits.
materials: Plain white paper (2 sheets per student)

section_titles: Line of symmetry and mirror line
periods.activity_title: Asymmetric flight: symmetry shapes how planes fly

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Making a paper airplane (d)–(h), p.165
tasks_in_class.description: Fly the symmetrical plane; try making an asymmetrical plane; fly both and observe which flies longer; share observations with friends.

time_bands.activity: Each student folds a fresh symmetric paper airplane following the textbook steps. The teacher asks the class to predict: 'If the two wings are exactly the same — mirror images of each other — what do you expect will happen when it flies?' Students share predictions with a partner before any test.

Students fly their symmetric planes across an open space in the classroom or corridor: Let Us Do, 2. Making a paper airplane (d)–(h), p.165 ("Fly symmetric plane; make asymmetric plane; fly both; observe which...."). They then deliberately crumple or bend one wing to make an asymmetric version and fly it. Students note on a small slip of paper: which flew straighter, which flew farther, and what they think explains the difference.

Class discussion: students share observations. The teacher collates responses on the board in two columns — symmetric / asymmetric — and draws out that a symmetric plane distributes force equally on both sides, helping it fly straight. Students use the words 'line of symmetry' and 'mirror line' in their explanations.

Students write one sentence in their notebooks: 'The symmetric plane flies _______ because _______.' Pairs read each other's sentences and decide whether they agree. This brief writing act fixes the connection between symmetry and balance.

periods.teacher_notes: The flying activity works best with a clear floor space; if the room is small, a corridor or verandah is preferable. Students sometimes make the asymmetric plane by folding it in a new way rather than just bending a wing — either approach is valid as long as the asymmetry is visible and they can articulate what changed. The key reasoning move is connecting equal halves to equal lift, so press for explanations rather than just results.
materials: Plain paper (1 sheet per student for the asymmetric plane)
Floor or corridor space for flying

section_titles: Holes and Cuts — fold-and-cut spatial reasoning
periods.activity_title: Predict the opening: fold-and-cut spatial puzzles

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, p.166
tasks_in_class.description: Take a square sheet of paper; fold and cut to reproduce Mini's design (fold twice, straight corner cut + two side squares removed).

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, Challenge 1, p.166
tasks_in_class.description: Predict where the hole and cut will appear when Rani's twice-folded paper (corner cut + two side squares) is opened.

time_bands.activity: Each student takes a square sheet and follows Mini's design: fold the paper twice (in half, then in half again), make a straight cut at the corner, and remove two small squares from the side edges: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, p.166 ("Fold twice; straight corner cut + two side squares removed...."). Students open the sheet and examine where the holes and cuts appear. The teacher asks: 'How many holes did you expect? How many did you get? Why?'

Challenge 1: students look at a drawing of Rani's twice-folded paper with a corner cut and two side-square removals — without cutting, they first sketch on blank paper where they predict the holes and cuts will appear when opened: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, Challenge 1, p.166 ("Predict where hole and cut appear when twice-folded paper is opened...."). After recording predictions, students make the actual cut and open the sheet to compare. Pairs discuss any mismatch and try to explain it using the idea of reflection.

Class debrief: three or four students share their prediction drawings alongside the actual opened sheet. The teacher highlights which folds acted as mirror lines and why each cut appeared in a mirrored position. The language 'mirror line', 'reflection', and 'symmetric' is used explicitly to describe what folding did to the cut.
Exit prompt: 'If a paper is folded twice and you make one cut at the corner, how many cut marks appear when you open it? Write your answer and a reason.' Students respond in one or two sentences.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error here is students forgetting that a twice-folded paper creates four layers, so one corner cut produces four corresponding marks when opened — explicitly counting layers before cutting helps. Encourage students to make predictions in sketch form before cutting so the reasoning is visible. Squared paper or grid paper for the prediction sketches gives students a reference grid that makes position easier to reason about.
materials: Square sheets of paper (2–3 per student)

section_titles: Holes and Cuts — fold-and-cut spatial reasoning
periods.activity_title: Middle cuts and square holes: spatial deduction deepens

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, Challenge 2, p.166
tasks_in_class.description: Fold a piece of paper once; put two cuts in the middle as shown. How many sides will the shape have when you open the folded paper?

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, Challenge 3, p.166
tasks_in_class.description: Fold a paper twice. Where would you cut to make a square hole in the centre? How many cuts are required?

time_bands.activity: Challenge 2: students fold a sheet once and look at the textbook diagram showing two mid-cuts on the folded edge: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, Challenge 2, p.166 ("Fold once; two mid-cuts as shown; count sides of shape when opened...."). They first predict: 'When I open this paper, what shape will the cut-out be? How many sides will it have?' Students sketch their prediction, then make the cuts and open the sheet. The class counts sides together and discusses whether the result was a surprise.

Challenge 3: students fold a paper twice and must plan — without cutting first — where to cut so that a square hole appears in the centre of the opened sheet: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, Challenge 3, p.166 ("Fold twice; plan and cut to make square hole in centre; count cuts...."). Students draw their planned cut on the folded shape, compare plans with a partner, then execute. Pairs who get different results unfold both and identify which strategy placed the cut correctly.

Whole-class consolidation: the teacher draws a folded paper on the board and asks: 'Which fold is the mirror line? If I cut here, where does it appear on the open sheet?' Students respond by pointing or drawing. The session closes by naming the principle: every fold acts as a line of symmetry, so cuts mirror across every fold.

periods.teacher_notes: Students tackling Challenge 3 often plan the cut at the corner of the twice-folded paper — remind them that the corner corresponds to the centre of the original sheet only when both folds pass through the centre; sketching the fold-layers helps locate the true centre. Challenge 2's two mid-cuts produce a rectangular cut-out strip when opened, not a hole; students counting sides should count the rectangle's four sides. Spare sheets allow students who make errors to retry without frustration.
materials: Square sheets of paper (3–4 per student)
Board or chart for teacher demonstration

section_titles: Symmetry in shapes, mirror games, and mirror writing
periods.activity_title: Dot-grid shapes and mirror games: seeing symmetry in 2D

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, Symmetry in shapes Q1, p.167
tasks_in_class.description: Draw the border shapes (kite, arrow, envelope, triangle) on the dot grid; identify which are symmetrical; draw the lines of symmetry.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Games with a Mirror Q2a, p.168
tasks_in_class.description: Where should the mirror be placed on shape A to produce each of the six given shapes (1–6)?

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Games with a Mirror Q2b, p.168
tasks_in_class.description: Circle the numbers (from: 181 vertical mirror, 181 horizontal mirror, 686 vertical, 686 horizontal) whose mirror image is the same number.

time_bands.activity: Students open to the dot-grid page and draw each of the four border shapes — kite, arrow, envelope, triangle — in the grid squares provided: Let Us Do, Symmetry in shapes Q1, p.167 ("Draw border shapes on dot grid; identify symmetrical; draw lines of symmetry...."). For each shape they decide: symmetrical or not? They draw the line of symmetry directly on the shape. Pairs compare and discuss any disagreement.

Distribute pocket mirrors. Students place a mirror on shape A in the textbook at different positions and orientations to generate each of the six derived shapes: Let Us Do, 2. Games with a Mirror Q2a, p.168 ("Place mirror on shape A to produce each of six given shapes...."). They record the mirror position (vertical, horizontal, diagonal) for each shape. The teacher circulates, asking: 'How did you decide where to put the mirror?'

Students place the mirror on the printed numbers 181 and 686 — first vertically, then horizontally — and decide which image 'is the same number': Let Us Do, 2. Games with a Mirror Q2b, p.168 ("Circle numbers whose mirror image is the same number...."). They circle correct cases and explain to a partner why the others change.

Quick oral close: the teacher holds the mirror vertically on a digit drawn on the board and asks: 'Does this digit look the same? Why or why not?' Two students explain. This bridges to the digit-symmetry exploration in the next task of this section.

periods.teacher_notes: Students familiar with symmetry in folded shapes may still be surprised that a shape can have more than one line of symmetry — the kite and triangle tasks surface this naturally, so press the question 'Could there be another line?' after the first line is drawn. For the mirror-number task, the most common error is confusing a vertical reflection with a horizontal one; labelling the mirror position each time prevents this. Ensure mirrors are clean and at a true right angle to the page for reliable reflections.
materials: Dot-grid paper or textbook dot-grid page
Pocket mirrors (one per student or pair)

section_titles: Symmetry in shapes, mirror games, and mirror writing
periods.activity_title: Mirror digits, mystery numbers, and ambulance writing

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Games with a Mirror Q2b extension, p.168
tasks_in_class.description: Which digits from 0 to 9 have the same mirror image? Make some 4-digit numbers whose mirror image is the same number; state where the mirror is kept.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Games with a Mirror Q2c, p.168
tasks_in_class.description: Make similar guess-my-number questions (e.g., 3-digit number near 120 with same mirror image) and ask friends to solve them.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Ambulance / mirror writing, p.169
tasks_in_class.description: Discuss why letters on an ambulance are written in reverse; identify mirror-written words (TAP, CAN, WOW, HEN); write words/names in mirror writing and challenge friends; try with your own language script.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 4. Complete symmetrical shapes, p.169
tasks_in_class.description: Complete the four half-shapes on the dot grid (two using a vertical axis, two using a horizontal axis) to make symmetrical figures.

time_bands.activity: Students write all digits 0–9 and test each with a mirror held vertically: Let Us Do, 2. Games with a Mirror Q2b extension, p.168 ("Which digits 0–9 have same mirror image? Make 4-digit numbers with same mirror image...."). They list the symmetric digits and then construct at least two 4-digit numbers using only those digits, placing the mirror and confirming the number reads the same.

Students compose their own 'Guess my number' clue — a 3-digit number near a given value whose mirror image is identical — and swap with a partner to solve: Let Us Do, 2. Games with a Mirror Q2c, p.168 ("Make guess-my-number questions; ask friends to solve them...."). The teacher collects two or three examples and works through them with the class, asking: 'How did you know only certain digits could appear?'

Ambulance discussion: the teacher sketches AMBULANCE in reverse on the board and asks why. Students share ideas, then read the textbook explanation about rear-view mirrors: Let Us Do, 3. Ambulance / mirror writing, p.169 ("Discuss why ambulance letters are reversed; identify mirror-written words; write names in mirror writing...."). Each student picks one word or their own name and writes it in mirror writing, then holds a mirror alongside to verify it reads correctly.

Students turn to the dot-grid half-shapes page and complete all four figures — two on a vertical axis, two on a horizontal axis: Let Us Do, 4. Complete symmetrical shapes, p.169 ("Complete four half-shapes on dot grid using vertical/horizontal axis...."). The teacher asks students to mark the axis of symmetry on each completed figure as the final step.

periods.teacher_notes: When students build 4-digit mirror numbers they often include digits like 2, 3, or 7, which are not symmetric — having the mirror available for each digit at the start prevents this error. For the ambulance activity, students from language backgrounds with non-Latin scripts can try mirror writing in their own script, which is a genuine and rich extension the textbook invites. The half-shape task on dot grids is good practice for counting dots carefully; a common error is overshooting the mirror axis by one dot, so ask students to mark the axis line first.

section_titles: Tiling the Tiles — tessellation and creative tile design
periods.activity_title: Tile patterns: repeating units, symmetry, and creative design

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 5. Observe shapes, p.170
tasks_in_class.description: Observe the given shapes; count sides for each; count lines of symmetry for each; trace and fold to verify lines of symmetry.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Tiling the Tiles Q1, p.171
tasks_in_class.description: Identify the repeating unit (tile) in each of the two given tile patterns and continue the patterns.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Tiling the Tiles Q2, p.171
tasks_in_class.description: Which shapes have you used to make the tiles? Which of the tiles are symmetrical? Draw the lines of symmetry if any.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Tiles at the Tile Shop, p.171
tasks_in_class.description: Design creative tiles of your own in the hexagonal and square spaces provided; use a rangometry kit or shape cutouts.

time_bands.activity: Students observe the given shapes on p.170 and work through the counting task: Let Us Do, 5. Observe shapes, p.170 ("Observe given shapes; count sides; count lines of symmetry; trace and fold to verify...."). They trace each shape onto plain paper, fold to find lines of symmetry, and compare their count with a partner. The teacher asks: 'Which shape has the most lines of symmetry? What do you notice?'

Students examine the two tile-pattern grids in the textbook and identify the repeating unit in each: Tiling the Tiles Q1, p.171 ("Identify repeating unit in two tile patterns; continue the patterns...."). They outline the repeating unit with a pencil, then continue the pattern by drawing or tracing. They then name the shapes used and mark lines of symmetry on one tile: Tiling the Tiles Q2, p.171 ("Which shapes used? Which tiles symmetrical? Draw lines of symmetry....").

Students turn to the 'Tiles at the Tile Shop' page and design their own tiles inside the hexagonal and square frames provided, using rangometry cutouts or hand-drawn shapes: Tiles at the Tile Shop, p.171 ("Design creative tiles in hexagonal/square spaces; use rangometry kit or cutouts...."). They colour their design and mark any lines of symmetry the tile has. Three or four students share their designs with the class, naming the shapes they used.

The teacher asks: 'Does a tile need to be symmetrical to tessellate — to cover the floor with no gaps?' Students offer quick yes/no responses with a reason, setting up the investigation to follow in the tiling tasks ahead.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes confuse the repeating unit with a single shape; help them circle the smallest group of shapes that, when repeated, produces the whole pattern. The creative tile design task works well if shape cutouts are available, but students who only have pencils can draw inside the frames directly — the key is choosing a design that could tile, not just a decorative picture. The closing question about whether symmetry is required for tessellation is intentionally left open here; the later activities in this section answer it concretely.

section_titles: Tiling the Tiles — tessellation and creative tile design
periods.activity_title: Floor patterns, rhombus designs, and the catty wall

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Tiles at the Tile Shop Q4, p.172
tasks_in_class.description: Look at the two rhombus/hexagon tessellation designs; discuss what you notice (shapes used, effect of colour, how colours create different visual patterns).

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 1. Make floor patterns, p.172
tasks_in_class.description: Make a floor pattern with your tile (like Mini's triangle-diamond pattern); ensure no overlaps and no gaps.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Making a catty wall, p.173
tasks_in_class.description: Take a square paper; mark cat ears/head outline; cut along outline; slide top piece down and tape; trace the cat tile to make a catty wall pattern with no gaps.

time_bands.activity: Students examine the two rhombus and hexagon tessellation designs on p.172: Tiles at the Tile Shop Q4, p.172 ("Look at rhombus/hexagon designs; discuss shapes, colour effect, different visual patterns...."). In pairs they discuss: which shapes are used, how colour changes the look even when the tile arrangement is the same, and whether the tiles are symmetrical. The teacher draws out responses — the same tessellation can look like cubes or flat diamonds depending on shading.

Students use the tile they designed in the previous work or a shape cutout to create a floor pattern on a blank sheet, tracing the tile repeatedly with no overlaps and no gaps: Let Us Do, 1. Make floor patterns, p.172 ("Make floor pattern with your tile; ensure no overlaps and no gaps...."). They colour their pattern. The teacher asks: 'Is your tile symmetrical? Does that change how it tessellates?'

Cat-tile activity: each student takes a square sheet, marks the cat head/ears outline at the top edge as shown in the textbook, cuts along the outline, slides the cut piece to the bottom edge, and tapes it to form the cat tile: Let Us Do, 2. Making a catty wall, p.173 ("Mark cat outline; cut; slide top piece down; tape; trace to make catty wall...."). Students trace the cat tile repeatedly to fill a blank sheet with the 'catty wall' pattern, confirming no gaps appear.

Class reflection: the teacher holds up a cat-tile sheet and asks 'Is this tile symmetric?' (it is not). 'Does it tessellate?' (yes). Students conclude that a tile does NOT need to be symmetric to tessellate — any shape that can slide to fill space without gaps works.

periods.teacher_notes: The rhombus-colour discussion is rich but can drift — keep the focus on what the mathematics shows (same tessellation, different perception) rather than purely aesthetic preference. For the catty wall, the slide-and-tape step is critical: students who cut and rotate rather than slide will not get the tessellating tile; demonstrate the slide motion slowly. A common error in the floor-pattern task is leaving small triangular gaps at corners; students should trace carefully and check each join.
materials: Square sheets of paper (2 per student)
Blank sheets for floor patterns and catty wall tracing

section_titles: Tiling the Tiles — tessellation and creative tile design
Nature walk — symmetry in the natural world
periods.activity_title: Tile extensions and a nature walk: symmetry outdoors

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Tiling the Tiles Q3, p.171
tasks_in_class.description: Make more tiles by joining two or more shapes; trace them in your notebook to create paths with no gaps or overlaps.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Let us go on a nature walk, p.174
tasks_in_class.description: Go on a nature walk; collect fallen leaves, petals, flowers; categorise as symmetrical/non-symmetrical; make designs and patterns; make a greeting card with leaf imprints; create animals or designs using leaves and flowers.

time_bands.activity: Students use shape cutouts or drawings to join two or more shapes into a new compound tile: Tiling the Tiles Q3, p.171 ("Join two or more shapes; trace in notebook; create paths with no gaps or overlaps...."). They trace the compound tile in their notebooks to create a continuous path pattern. The teacher asks: 'What shapes did you combine? Does the combined tile tessellate better or worse than either shape alone?'

Nature walk: students move outside (school garden, courtyard, or a designated area) and collect fallen leaves, petals, and flowers — only those already on the ground: Let Us Do, 3. Let us go on a nature walk, p.174 ("Collect fallen leaves, petals, flowers; categorise as symmetrical/non-symmetrical; make designs; make leaf-imprint greeting card...."). Each student collects five to eight items. Back at their seats they sort the collection into two groups — symmetrical and non-symmetrical — and describe what they used to decide.

Students choose two or three leaves from their symmetrical group, press them onto a folded card with paint or by rubbing a pencil over the leaf surface, and create a leaf-imprint greeting card. They may also arrange loose leaves and flowers into an animal or pattern design on their desk, then sketch it in their notebook. Each student labels one leaf 'symmetrical' and draws its line of symmetry on the sketch.

periods.teacher_notes: Arrange outdoor permissions and supervision in advance; if an outdoor walk is not possible, a set of leaf cut-outs or printed leaf images can substitute, but the tactile sorting experience is worth organising. Students categorising leaves sometimes decide by shape alone without checking both halves carefully — encourage them to fold the actual leaf along its midrib to test. The greeting-card task is intentionally brief and closes within this sitting; no continuation is needed.
materials: Shape cutouts or tracing paper for the tile task
Paint or washable ink pads for leaf imprints
Folded card or thick paper for greeting cards
Bags or trays for collecting natural materials

section_titles: Line of symmetry and mirror line
Holes and Cuts — fold-and-cut spatial reasoning
Symmetry in shapes, mirror games, and mirror writing
Tiling the Tiles — tessellation and creative tile design
Nature walk — symmetry in the natural world
periods.activity_title: Symmetry everywhere: a whole-chapter gallery and challenge

time_bands.activity: Symmetry warm-up gallery: the teacher displays five objects or drawings on the board — an ink-blot design, a folded-paper cut, a dot-grid shape, a tile pattern, and a leaf sketch. Students move around, identify the line of symmetry (or its absence) on each, and write one word describing what kind of symmetry work each represents (folding, cutting, tiling, nature). This quick survey reactivates every strand of the chapter.

Three-station rotation (groups of roughly equal size rotate once at the midpoint of this band): Station A — fold a fresh sheet twice and predict where a single corner cut lands, then verify; Station B — place a mirror on a printed shape (teacher-drawn on a card) to produce a target reflection and describe mirror position; Station C — look at a two-shape compound tile (teacher-drawn) and decide whether it tessellates, then test by tracing. Each station revisits one major concept strand: fold-and-cut reasoning from the holes-and-cuts work, mirror placement from the mirror games, and tessellation from the tiling work.

Whole-class challenge: the teacher poses three rapid questions connecting the chapter's ideas — (1) 'Name a digit that has mirror symmetry and use it to build a 3-digit number that looks the same in a vertical mirror.' (2) 'A leaf is folded along its midrib and the two halves match exactly — what does that tell us?' (3) 'A cat-shaped tile tessellates even though it is not symmetric — true or false? Explain.' Students write their answers and reasons in notebooks, then two or three students share each answer for class discussion.

Student self-summary: each student writes two sentences — one naming the most surprising thing they discovered about symmetry across the chapter's activities, and one giving an example of symmetry they would look for outside the classroom. Volunteers share. The teacher closes by connecting the chapter's thread: folding, cutting, mirroring, tiling, and nature walks are all ways of meeting the same mathematical idea — a line of symmetry — in different materials and settings.

periods.teacher_notes: The three stations need minimal materials prepared in advance — folded-paper and scissors at Station A, a mirror and a teacher-drawn shape card at Station B, and a tile sketch on plain paper at Station C; nothing from earlier sittings is required. The three rapid challenge questions in the whole-class segment synthesise mirror digits from the symmetry-in-shapes section, leaf symmetry from the nature walk, and the catty-wall conclusion from the tiling work — press students to use the chapter's vocabulary (line of symmetry, mirror line, tessellate) in their explanations. Encourage students whose self-summary sentence mentions an outdoor example to name it specifically — a temple floor, a rangoli, a butterfly wing — since connecting the concept to their own world is the chapter's deepest goal.
materials: Plain sheets for folding and cutting (Station A)
Pocket mirrors and teacher-drawn shape cards (Station B)
Tile sketch on plain paper and pencils (Station C)
Board or display surface for the opening gallery

items.section_title: Line of symmetry and mirror line
items.prompt: Meena folded a square piece of paper exactly in half and pressed a blob of red paint near the fold. She opened the paper and saw a design. Draw what you think the design looks like and mark the line of symmetry on your drawing.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student's drawing should show a design that is the same on both sides of a central fold line, with the fold line marked as the line of symmetry.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Folding paper in half means both sides are mirror images of each other across the fold, which is the line of symmetry.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold and press paper with paint to see it directly; stretch: ask them to predict and draw what two blobs at different distances from the fold would look like.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 1. Ink Design, p.164
exercise.description: Fold a sheet of paper in half, sprinkle water-colour drops at the fold, press to spread colour, open and observe the symmetrical ink design produced.

items.section_title: Line of symmetry and mirror line
items.prompt: Ravi made a symmetric paper airplane. He then bent one wing upward so the two wings were no longer the same. What is most likely to happen when he flies the bent plane compared to the symmetric one?

options.label: A
options.text: Both planes will behave exactly the same because the paper is the same.

options.label: B
options.text: The bent plane will curve or wobble because the two sides are unequal.

options.label: C
options.text: The bent plane will fly higher because one wing catches more air.

options.label: D
options.text: The bent plane will fly in a straight line just like the symmetric one.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The bent plane will curve or wobble because the two sides are unequal.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A symmetric plane has equal halves that push against air equally, giving straight flight; removing symmetry makes the two sides push differently, causing veering.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student does not connect symmetry of the plane to balance of forces, thinking shape change does not affect flight.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student thinks more surface area on one side increases height rather than causing imbalance.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student focuses on material rather than shape, missing that the geometry of the wings determines flight behaviour.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold and bend a plane themselves and fly both versions; stretch: ask what other changes to the plane (e.g. unequal tail flaps) would also break symmetry and affect flight.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Making a paper airplane (d)–(h), p.165
exercise.description: Fly the symmetrical plane; try making an asymmetrical plane; fly both and observe which flies longer; share observations with friends.

items.section_title: Holes and Cuts — fold-and-cut spatial reasoning
items.prompt: Priya took a square sheet of paper, folded it in half once, and cut a small triangle from the folded edge. She opened the sheet. Describe what the cut-out looks like and explain why it has that shape.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The cut-out is a diamond (rhombus) shape — two triangles joined at their bases — because the fold reflects the triangular cut to the other side, producing a symmetric shape.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A fold acts as a line of symmetry; cutting a triangle from the folded edge mirrors that cut to create an identical triangle on the other side, forming a diamond when opened.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold and cut the paper themselves before describing; stretch: ask what shape appears if the cut is a semicircle instead of a triangle.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, p.166
exercise.description: Take a square sheet of paper; fold and cut to reproduce Mini's design (fold twice, straight corner cut + two side squares removed).

items.section_title: Symmetry in shapes, mirror games, and mirror writing
items.prompt: The word AMBULANCE is painted in mirror writing on the front of an ambulance. Why is it written that way?

options.label: A
options.text: Because ambulance drivers prefer decorative lettering on their vehicles.

options.label: B
options.text: So that a driver looking in their rear-view mirror sees the word the right way around.

options.label: C
options.text: So that people walking on the road can read it easily from the front.

options.label: D
options.text: So that the word takes up less space on the front of the vehicle.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: So that a driver looking in their rear-view mirror sees the word the right way around.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A rear-view mirror reverses left and right; writing AMBULANCE in reverse compensates so the mirror image reads correctly.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student thinks the audience is pedestrians looking at the front directly, missing the role of the rear-view mirror.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student attributes the choice to aesthetics rather than function, not connecting mirror writing to reflection.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student focuses on space rather than readability, showing no connection to the mirror-image concept.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to write their name normally and then hold a mirror beside it to see what a rear-view mirror does; stretch: ask which other letters of the alphabet look the same in a mirror and why those do not need reversing.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Ambulance / mirror writing, p.169
exercise.description: Discuss why letters on an ambulance are written in reverse; identify mirror-written words (TAP, CAN, WOW, HEN); write words/names in mirror writing and challenge friends; try with your own language script.

items.section_title: Tiling the Tiles — tessellation and creative tile design
items.prompt: Sunita wants to design her own tile using two different shapes joined together. She joins a square and an equilateral triangle along one edge. Draw this compound tile and mark any lines of symmetry it has.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The compound tile is a pentagon (a square with a triangle on top of one side). It has one line of symmetry — a vertical line passing through the midpoint of the shared edge and the apex of the triangle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold the compound shape along the vertical centre line; the square's left and right halves match, and the triangle's two halves match, so the vertical centre is the one line of symmetry.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student cut out a square and triangle from paper, join them, and fold to find the symmetry line; stretch: ask them to try attaching the triangle to a corner edge instead and check whether the symmetry line changes.

exercise.book_ref: Tiles at the Tile Shop, p.171
exercise.description: Design creative tiles of your own in the hexagonal and square spaces provided; use a rangometry kit or shape cutouts.

items.section_title: Tiling the Tiles — tessellation and creative tile design
items.prompt: Karan made a cat-shaped tile by cutting from a square piece of paper and sliding the cut piece to the opposite edge. He then traced this tile again and again to fill a page. Is the cat tile symmetric? Can it cover a surface with no gaps? Write one sentence for each answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The cat tile is not symmetric because the cut-and-slide process creates an irregular outline with no line of symmetry. It can still cover a surface with no gaps because the bumps on one side fit exactly into the dents on the next tile when slid into place.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A tile tessellates when its edges fit together without gaps, regardless of whether the tile is symmetric; the cut-slide-paste method ensures matching bumps and dents.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student make and trace the cat tile from a real square sheet to see the fit; stretch: ask whether rotating the cat tile 180° still lets it tessellate, or whether only sliding works.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Making a catty wall, p.173
exercise.description: Take a square paper; mark cat ears/head outline; cut along outline; slide top piece down and tape; trace the cat tile to make a catty wall pattern with no gaps.

items.section_title: Nature walk — symmetry in the natural world
items.prompt: Deepa collected four leaves on a nature walk. She folded each leaf along its midrib (the main central vein) to check for symmetry. Which description best shows a symmetric leaf?

options.label: A
options.text: One half is jagged and the other half is smooth when folded.

options.label: B
options.text: The leaf has no midrib at all.

options.label: C
options.text: The two halves are very different sizes when folded.

options.label: D
options.text: The two halves match almost exactly when folded along the midrib.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The two halves match almost exactly when folded along the midrib.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A leaf is symmetric when its midrib acts as a line of symmetry so that folding produces two matching halves.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student associates symmetry with a fold mark rather than matching halves, not understanding what the fold test checks.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student does not connect matching outlines to symmetry, focusing on texture differences instead.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student conflates the presence of a midrib with symmetry, not understanding that the midrib is merely where you fold to test.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student two leaves and ask them to fold each and feel whether the edges line up; stretch: ask them to find a leaf that is nearly but not perfectly symmetric and explain what breaks the symmetry.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Let us go on a nature walk, p.174
exercise.description: Go on a nature walk; collect fallen leaves, petals, flowers; categorise as symmetrical/non-symmetrical; make designs and patterns; make a greeting card with leaf imprints; create animals or designs using leaves and flowers.

items.section_title: Line of symmetry and mirror line
items.prompt: A paper airplane is folded so that both wings are exactly the same — each wing is a mirror image of the other. How many lines of symmetry does the finished plane have, and where is each line? Explain your reasoning.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The finished plane has one line of symmetry — the central fold line that runs from nose to tail. The two wings are mirror images of each other across this line.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether the shape on one side of a fold line is an exact reflection of the shape on the other side; the central fold of the plane is the only line where this holds.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold a piece of paper and hold a mirror along different lines to see which gives matching halves; stretch: ask whether the plane would still have the same symmetry line if one wing were wider than the other.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Making a paper airplane (a)–(c), p.165
exercise.description: Mark the line of symmetry in Fig. 3, 4, and 5; count how many lines of symmetry Fig. 8 has; decide where to place a mirror to see the right-half reflection and whether it matches the left half.

items.section_title: Holes and Cuts — fold-and-cut spatial reasoning
items.prompt: Arun folded a square sheet in half once and then cut a small square from the corner that is NOT on the fold. When he opens the sheet, what does the cut look like?

options.label: A
options.text: A square hole in the middle of the sheet.

options.label: B
options.text: Four square notches, one at each corner of the sheet.

options.label: C
options.text: One small square notch cut from one corner only.

options.label: D
options.text: Two small square notches, one on each of two opposite corners.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Two small square notches, one on each of two opposite corners.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The fold creates two layers; cutting the free corner removes a square from both layers simultaneously, so opening the sheet reveals two notches at positions that are mirror images across the fold line.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student does not account for the fold creating a second layer and thinks only one layer is cut.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses a corner cut with a centred cut, imagining the cut lands in the middle when the sheet is opened.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student over-counts the layers, perhaps imagining a twice-folded sheet or thinking every corner is affected.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold a sheet, make the cut, and open it to count notches; stretch: ask where the notches would be if the cut were from the corner ON the fold instead.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, Challenge 1, p.166
exercise.description: Predict where the hole and cut will appear when Rani's twice-folded paper (corner cut + two side squares) is opened.

items.section_title: Holes and Cuts — fold-and-cut spatial reasoning
items.prompt: A sheet of paper is folded once and two cuts are made side by side in the middle of the folded edge, removing a rectangular strip. How many sides does the hole have when the sheet is opened? Explain how you worked it out.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The hole has 4 sides — it is a rectangle. The two cuts remove a strip from the folded edge; when opened, the strip from both layers produces a rectangular hole with four straight sides.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Each pair of parallel cuts on the folded sheet produces two parallel edges; the fold mirrors them to give the other two parallel edges, forming a rectangle.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold and make the cuts to count sides directly; stretch: ask what shape the hole would be if the two cuts were not parallel but angled toward each other.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, Challenge 2, p.166
exercise.description: Fold a piece of paper once; put two cuts in the middle as shown. How many sides will the shape have when you open the folded paper?

items.section_title: Holes and Cuts — fold-and-cut spatial reasoning
items.prompt: Sana folded a square sheet of paper in half twice (first left-to-right, then top-to-bottom). She wants a square hole exactly in the centre of the opened sheet. Where should she cut, and how many cuts does she need?

options.label: A
options.text: Cut anywhere on the folded paper; the hole will always land in the centre.

options.label: B
options.text: Cut at the corner where all four layers meet; one cut is enough.

options.label: C
options.text: Cut at the middle of one folded edge; two cuts are needed.

options.label: D
options.text: Cut from the outer corner (free edges); one diagonal cut is enough.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Cut at the corner where all four layers meet; one cut is enough.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: When a sheet is folded twice through its centre, the corner that has all four layers corresponds to the centre of the original sheet; one cut there opens to a centred hole.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student confuses a mid-edge cut (which produces an edge notch) with a centred hole, not tracking where the fold lines place the centre.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student does not connect the position of the cut on the folded sheet to the position of the hole on the opened sheet.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student thinks a diagonal outer-corner cut lands centrally, not realising the free-edge corner maps to an outer corner of the open sheet.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold and feel which corner has all layers, then make the cut and open to check; stretch: ask how the answer changes if the two folds do not go through the centre of the sheet.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, Challenge 3, p.166
exercise.description: Fold a paper twice. Where would you cut to make a square hole in the centre? How many cuts are required?

items.section_title: Symmetry in shapes, mirror games, and mirror writing
items.prompt: Look at these four shapes: a kite, an arrow, a rectangle, and a circle. Which of these shapes has more than one line of symmetry? For each such shape, state how many lines of symmetry it has.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry (one vertical, one horizontal). The circle has infinitely many lines of symmetry (any diameter). The kite and arrow each have only 1 line of symmetry.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Test each candidate line by checking whether folding along it makes the two halves match exactly; count every line where this works.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student cut out each shape and fold in different directions to find matching halves; stretch: ask whether a square has more lines of symmetry than a rectangle and to draw all of them.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, Symmetry in shapes Q1, p.167
exercise.description: Draw the border shapes (kite, arrow, envelope, triangle) on the dot grid; identify which are symmetrical; draw the lines of symmetry.

items.section_title: Symmetry in shapes, mirror games, and mirror writing
items.prompt: Which of the following 4-digit numbers looks exactly the same when you hold a vertical mirror to its right side?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Only the digits 0 and 1 have a symmetric mirror image when a vertical mirror is used; 1001 uses only these digits, so its vertical mirror image is 1001 reversed — which is also 1001.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may think 8 is a symmetric digit in a vertical mirror, but a vertical mirror of 8 is still 8, yet 1801 reversed is 1081, not 1801, so the number as a whole is not the same.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has not checked which individual digits are symmetric in a vertical mirror; digits 2, 3, and 4 are not symmetric.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may think 8 is vertically symmetric (it is) but does not check whether the whole number reads the same when reversed; 8018 reversed is 8108, not 8018.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student test each digit 0–9 with a mirror and list symmetric ones before trying the number; stretch: ask the student to construct their own 4-digit vertically symmetric number different from those given.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Games with a Mirror Q2b extension, p.168
exercise.description: Which digits from 0 to 9 have the same mirror image? Make some 4-digit numbers whose mirror image is the same number; state where the mirror is kept.

items.section_title: Tiling the Tiles — tessellation and creative tile design
items.prompt: A student says: 'A tile must be symmetric to tessellate — to cover a floor with no gaps.' Do you agree? Use the shapes you know from the chapter to explain your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student is wrong. A tile does not need to be symmetric to tessellate. The cat-shaped tile made by the cut-slide-paste method is an example — it is not symmetric but it covers a surface with no gaps because the bumps on one side fit exactly into the dents of the neighbouring tile.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Tessellation depends on edges fitting together without gaps, not on the tile having a line of symmetry.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: show the student a symmetric tile (square) and an asymmetric tile (the cat tile) and ask them to trace each repeatedly to see which leaves gaps; stretch: ask whether every symmetric tile tessellates — think of a circle, which is symmetric but does not tile without gaps.

exercise.description: Identify the repeating unit (tile) in each of the two given tile patterns and continue the patterns.

items.section_title: Tiling the Tiles — tessellation and creative tile design
items.prompt: A regular hexagon has 6 sides. How many lines of symmetry does it have? Describe where each line goes.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A regular hexagon has 6 lines of symmetry: 3 lines each connect midpoints of opposite sides, and 3 lines each connect opposite vertices (corners).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Trace the hexagon, fold along each candidate line, and check whether the halves match; a regular hexagon folds symmetrically along 3 vertex-to-vertex lines and 3 midpoint-to-midpoint lines.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student trace and cut out a hexagon, then fold in different directions to count matching folds; stretch: ask how the number of symmetry lines would change if the hexagon were irregular (not all sides equal).

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 5. Observe shapes, p.170
exercise.description: Observe the given shapes; count sides for each; count lines of symmetry for each; trace and fold to verify lines of symmetry.

items.section_title: Symmetry in shapes, mirror games, and mirror writing
items.prompt: Here is a 'Guess my number' clue: I am a 3-digit number. My mirror image (with a vertical mirror on my right) is exactly the same number. All my digits are the same. What number am I?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Only digit 1 has a symmetric vertical mirror image (1 reversed is still 1); a three-digit number with all digits the same and using only vertically symmetric digits must be 111.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may think 2 is symmetric in a vertical mirror, but a vertical mirror of 2 produces a reversed 2, which is not the same digit.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may think 3 is symmetric in a vertical mirror, but 3 reversed is a different shape.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student correctly identifies 8 as vertically symmetric but does not notice the clue says all digits are the same — 888 has a vertical mirror image of 888, so this is actually a valid answer too; if the teacher uses this item, accept 888 as well or revise the clue to exclude it.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a list of vertically symmetric digits (0, 1, 8) and ask which three-digit number with all identical digits can be formed; stretch: ask the student to write their own 'Guess my number' clue for a 3-digit number using two different symmetric digits.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Games with a Mirror Q2c, p.168
exercise.description: Make similar guess-my-number questions (e.g., 3-digit number near 120 with same mirror image) and ask friends to solve them.

items.section_title: Symmetry in shapes, mirror games, and mirror writing
items.prompt: The dot grid below shows half of a shape. The dashed line is the vertical line of symmetry. Complete the other half of the shape so that the whole figure is symmetric.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The completed shape has the right half mirror the left half across the central vertical column: the pattern of filled dots (* marks) on the right side of the axis matches the pattern on the left side in reverse order.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: For each filled dot on one side of the axis, count its distance from the axis and place a matching dot at the same distance on the other side.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold the dot-grid paper along the axis line and press to transfer the marks to the other side; stretch: ask the student to create their own half-shape on a dot grid for a partner to complete.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 4. Complete symmetrical shapes, p.169
exercise.description: Complete the four half-shapes on the dot grid (two using a vertical axis, two using a horizontal axis) to make symmetrical figures.
